content.body: Have you ever had to quickly access something you recently used, like a favorite tool or a recent file? An LRU Cache helps computers do exactly that—keep frequently used items ready for instant access. In this lesson, we'll build one using arrays and hashmaps to remember what we've seen and manage limited space efficiently.
content.title: Introduction

content.body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
1. Explain how an LRU Cache uses a hashmap for fast lookups and a list to track usage order.
2. Implement the core operations: get (retrieve) and put (add/update) items in the cache.
3. Apply the 'remember what we have already seen' mental model to manage cache capacity by removing the least recently used item.
content.title: What you'll learn
Try it
content.prompt: Imagine a tiny cache that can only hold 2 items. We add items A, B, then access A. Which item gets removed if we add C?
content.successMessage: Correct! Since A was recently accessed, B is the least recently used and gets removed.

content.title: Try a bigger cache
content.prompt: Now a cache holds 3 items. We add X, Y, Z, access X, then add W. Which item gets removed?
content.successMessage: Well done! X was accessed, so Y is the least recently used among Y and Z.

content.title: One more
content.prompt: Cache size 4: add 1, 2, 3, 4, access 2, access 1, add 5. Which item gets removed?
content.successMessage: Great! You tracked usage: after accesses, 3 is the least recently used.

content.body: What you just did was manually track the order of usage in your mind. You checked which items were accessed recently and which were not. For a small cache, this works, but for a computer managing thousands of items, we need a systematic way to remember what we've seen and quickly identify the least recently used.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When the cache has to handle many items and frequent accesses, keeping track of usage order manually becomes impossible. We need a data structure that can quickly look up items and update their recency. Can't figure out how? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: The core idea is to remember what we have already seen using a lookup structure. For an LRU Cache, we use a hashmap (like a JavaScript Map) to store items for instant access, and a list (like an array or linked list) to track the order of usage. The hashmap lets us check if an item exists in one step, and the list helps us know which item to remove when the cache is full.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Think of it as a notebook where we write down what we've seen and check it in one step. The notebook has two parts: a quick index (hashmap) to find items, and a timeline (list) showing when each item was last used.

content.body: We'll combine a Map for fast lookups and an array to maintain usage order. When we access an item, we move it to the 'most recent' position. When adding a new item to a full cache, we remove the one at the 'least recent' position.
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample: Walkthrough with cache size 2: Put A → Map: {A}, List: [A]. Put B → Map: {A, B}, List: [A, B]. Get A → Move A to end: List: [B, A]. Put C (full) → Remove least recent (B) from list and map, add C: Map: {A, C}, List: [A, C].

content.body:
1. Initialize the cache with a maximum capacity, an empty Map, and an empty array for order.
2. For get(key): if key exists in Map, move it to the end of the array (most recent) and return its value; else return -1.
3. For put(key, value): if key exists, update its value and move to end; else if cache is full, remove the first item from array (least recent) and delete from Map, then add new key to Map and end of array.
4. Always ensure the array length does not exceed capacity.
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Create the LRUCache class
steps.instruction: Define a class LRUCache with a constructor that takes capacity. Initialize this.capacity, this.cache (a Map), and this.order (an array) to track usage.
steps.expectedOutcome: Class defined with capacity, cache Map, and order array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've set up the basic structure for the cache.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure to initialize all three properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. The class needs capacity, a Map for cache, and an array for order.

steps.title: Implement get method - check existence
steps.instruction: Add a get(key) method. If key exists in this.cache, return its value; otherwise return -1. Don't update order yet.
steps.hint: Use this.cache.has(key) to check, and this.cache.get(key) to retrieve value.
steps.expectedOutcome: get method returns value if key exists, else -1.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You can now check if an item is in the cache.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost. Ensure you return the value if key exists, and -1 otherwise.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember: check this.cache.has(key), then return value or -1.

steps.title: Update order on get
steps.instruction: Extend get(key) to update usage order. If key exists, move it to the end of this.order (most recent). Hint: remove from array, then push.
steps.hint: Find index with this.order.indexOf(key), splice to remove, then push key.
steps.expectedOutcome: get method now moves accessed key to end of order array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! Now the cache tracks recent accesses.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start. Make sure to remove key from its current position and add to end.
steps.feedbackWrong: Think: find index, splice it out, then push key to order.

steps.title: Implement put method - add new item
steps.instruction: Add a put(key, value) method. If key does not exist and cache is not full, add to this.cache and end of this.order.
steps.hint: Check if key exists with this.cache.has(key). If not and this.order.length < this.capacity, add.
steps.expectedOutcome: put adds new key-value pair to cache and order when capacity allows.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! You can now add items to the cache.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check both conditions: key doesn't exist and cache isn't full.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember: use this.cache.set(key, value) and this.order.push(key).

steps.title: Handle cache full in put
steps.instruction: Extend put to handle full cache. If key doesn't exist and cache is full, remove least recent from this.order (first item) and delete from this.cache, then add new item.
steps.hint: Least recent is this.order[0]. Remove it from array and Map before adding new.
steps.expectedOutcome: put now evicts least recently used item when full before adding new.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Well done! The cache now manages capacity correctly.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost. Remove the first item from order and delete from cache.
steps.feedbackWrong: Think: if full, get this.order[0], delete from cache, shift from order, then add new.

steps.title: Update existing key in put
steps.instruction: Finalize put: if key already exists, update its value in this.cache and move to end of this.order (like get).
steps.hint: Reuse the order update logic from get when key exists.
steps.expectedOutcome: put fully handles both new and existing keys with order updates.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! Your LRU Cache is complete and efficient.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good. When key exists, update value and move to end of order.
steps.feedbackWrong: For existing key: set new value, then update order similar to get.

content.body: Congratulations! You've built an LRU Cache from scratch. Remember: the hashmap (Map) gives us instant lookups, and the array tracks usage order to remember what we've already seen. This combination allows efficient management of limited cache space by always removing the least recently used item. Keep practicing this 'remember what we have seen' pattern—it's powerful for many algorithms!
content.title: Done
